title: Handle your first customer ticket well
goal: You will triage, investigate, answer, document, and resolve one real customer support ticket.
prerequisites: A new ticket assigned to your support queue
Access to your team's approved help articles and policies

steps.action: Open the new customer ticket from the ticket queue.
steps.where: Left navigation bar > Views icon > Unassigned tickets or your team's new-ticket view > ticket subject.
steps.why: Opening the ticket reveals the customer's message and its current status.
steps.checkpoint: You should see the ticket subject, conversation thread, requester details, and reply composer.
hint_levels: Start with the Views icon in the left navigation bar.
Open the view containing new tickets, then find the customer's ticket by its subject.
Click Views, click Unassigned tickets or your team's new-ticket view, then click the ticket subject.

steps.where: Ticket properties panel on the left > Assignee field.
steps.why: Assignment shows your team that you own the next response.
steps.checkpoint: You should see your name in the Assignee field.
hint_levels: Look through the ticket properties on the left.
The Assignee dropdown controls who owns the ticket.
Click Assignee, search for your name, then click your name.

steps.action: Set the ticket type and priority from the customer's stated issue and impact.
steps.where: Ticket properties panel on the left > Type and Priority dropdowns.
steps.why: Accurate triage helps the team route and order work consistently.
steps.checkpoint: You should see selected values in both the Type and Priority fields.
hint_levels: Focus on what the customer needs and how severely it affects them.
Choose the matching Type, then use your team's impact rules to choose Priority.
Click Type and select Question, Incident, Problem, or Task; then click Priority and select Low, Normal, High, or Urgent.

steps.action: Review the requester's profile and previous tickets for relevant account details or recurring issues.
steps.where: Requester context panel on the right > User profile and Interaction history or Tickets tabs.
steps.why: Past context can prevent repeated questions and reveal whether the issue is isolated or recurring.
steps.checkpoint: You should see the customer's profile details and a list of prior interactions or tickets, even if the list is empty.
hint_levels: Check the customer context beside the conversation.
The requester panel contains profile information and previous interactions.
In the right requester panel, expand User profile, then click Interaction history or Tickets and review the entries.

steps.action: Search the Knowledge Capture panel for an approved article that matches the issue.
steps.where: Ticket workspace right sidebar > Knowledge icon > search field.
steps.why: An approved source gives you accurate troubleshooting steps and policy language.
steps.checkpoint: You should see search results containing at least one relevant help article or a clear no-results message.
hint_levels: Use the knowledge tools beside the ticket.
Search with the product name plus the customer's main symptom.
Click the Knowledge icon in the right sidebar, click the search field, type the product and symptom, then press Enter.

steps.action: Add an internal note summarizing the issue, impact, evidence checked, and planned resolution.
steps.where: Reply composer at the bottom of the conversation > Public reply dropdown > Internal note.
steps.why: A concise investigation record lets teammates understand and continue the work.
steps.checkpoint: You should see a yellow Internal note entry in the conversation containing your summary.
hint_levels: Document your reasoning without sending it to the customer.
Switch the composer from Public reply to Internal note and record the four key facts.
Click Public reply, select Internal note, type the issue, impact, evidence checked, and planned resolution, then click Submit as Open.

steps.action: Write a public reply that acknowledges the problem, states the answer or next steps, and sets a clear expectation.
steps.where: Reply composer at the bottom of the conversation > response text box.
steps.why: A clear and empathetic response helps the customer act without guessing what happens next.
steps.checkpoint: You should see a drafted reply that includes an acknowledgment, specific guidance, and an expected outcome or timeframe.
hint_levels: Write for the customer, not for your internal team.
Open with acknowledgment, give numbered actions or a direct answer, and end with what the customer should expect.
Select Public reply, then type a greeting, acknowledgment, solution or next steps, expectation, and courteous closing.

steps.action: Proofread the public reply against the original request and remove jargon, unsupported promises, and unnecessary details.
steps.where: Conversation thread and Public reply composer at the bottom of the ticket.
steps.why: A final comparison catches tone errors and ensures every customer question is answered.
steps.checkpoint: You should see a concise draft that answers each customer question and contains no internal notes or unexplained abbreviations.
hint_levels: Compare the draft with the customer's first message.
Check accuracy, completeness, tone, and whether every next step is concrete.
Read the original message, reread the Public reply draft, then edit any unclear, missing, or overly technical wording.

steps.action: Send the reply with the ticket status set to Solved.
steps.where: Bottom-right of the ticket > Submit as status dropdown and Submit button.
steps.why: Solving records the completed outcome while allowing the customer to reopen the ticket by replying.
steps.checkpoint: You should see the public reply in the conversation and the ticket status displayed as Solved.
hint_levels: Use the submission control beside the reply composer.
Choose Solved only if your response fully answers the issue and no internal work remains.
Click the arrow beside Submit as, select Solved, then click Submit as Solved.
